narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 73.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being ranked in the bottom decile in both your first and third years of law school signaled a much higher risk compared to accepted students, who on average ranked around the middle of their class (roughly 6th decile). This consistent low performance outweighed other information the model considered.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor and worked in your favor. At 3.80 it is well above the 3.23 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction toward passing. However, this positive signal was not enough to overcome the impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 39 was actually slightly above the accepted average of 37.2, your upper-middle family income is common among accepted applicants, and your status as a full-time female white student played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and class standing in law school. Consider seeking additional academic support, tutoring, or study strategies that can help you rank higher in your remaining courses. This would directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction. (248 words)
